name: Twin Sepulchers

stars.name: The Elder Pall
stars.notes: Hydrogen-atmosphere white dwarf, the more massive of the pair. Surface temperature approximately 12,000 K. Orbital period around common center of mass is 4.7 hours.

stars.name: The Younger Pall
stars.notes: Cool, featureless white dwarf with no detectable spectral lines. Surface temperature approximately 5,200 K. Nearly invisible to the naked eye despite being a stellar object.

planets.name: Epitaph
planets.notes: Circumbinary world in a wide, stable orbit. Tidally stressed by the binary pair, its surface is a maze of fractures. Contains deposits of an anomalous crystalline material that does not match any known mineral.

planets.name: Requiescat
planets.notes: Outer circumbinary world with a retrograde moon. Surface is featureless regolith except for a single massive depression—a perfectly circular basin 800 km in diameter and 12 km deep. Not consistent with impact geology.

anomalies.name: The Basin
anomalies.notes: Circular depression with mathematically perfect geometry, 800 km diameter, 12 km depth. Walls are smooth to within centimeters. Material was not displaced but appears to have been removed entirely—no ejecta, no rim deposits. Estimated age: 4 billion years.

anomalies.name: Mourning Glass
anomalies.notes: Crystalline material filling fractures in Epitaph's crust. Exhibits negative thermal expansion—it grows when cooled and shrinks when heated. Does not correspond to any known mineral or synthetic compound. Possibly deposited by the same intelligence that created The Basin.

faction_control.notes: Unclaimed. The system appears on Exploration Guild charts as a navigational waypoint only. No faction has expressed interest in establishing a presence.

history: The binary pair was identified in 2351 by automated spectroscopic survey. The system was flagged as unremarkable—two cooling stellar corpses with minimal planetary material.

A passing research vessel conducted a cursory scan in 2478 and discovered The Basin on Requiescat. The finding was published in a minor journal and largely ignored due to the system's inaccessibility and lack of funding for follow-up.

Mourning Glass was identified in 2534 when an independent prospector landed on Epitaph hoping to find exotic metals. The crystalline material's anomalous properties were documented but have attracted only sporadic academic attention.
description: Two dead stars orbit each other in a tight, eternal waltz—one white and fading, the other so dim it barely registers on sensors. The Twin Sepulchers is a binary graveyard where two stars that exhausted their fuel billions of years apart now share a common grave, circling their mutual center of mass once every 4.7 hours. The two surviving planets orbit the pair at safe distances, cold and airless witnesses to the slow cooling of their suns.

The system's anomalies are subtle but deeply strange. The Basin on Requiescat is not an impact crater—there is no ejecta, no shattered rock, no deformation consistent with collision. Something removed 800 kilometers of material to a depth of 12 kilometers with surgical precision and took it somewhere else entirely. On Epitaph, Mourning Glass fills the planet's fractures with a substance that should not exist according to known materials science. These are not the marks of nature. They are the marks of capability so far beyond human technology that the distinction between engineering and magic becomes academic.

No one comes to the Twin Sepulchers. The binary white dwarfs offer no energy worth harvesting, the planets hold no resources worth extracting, and the anomalies resist analysis with the placid stubbornness of deep time. The Basin waits with its perfect geometry. The Mourning Glass grows in the cold. Two stars die together in the dark, and whatever once worked here has been gone so long that even asking who they were feels presumptuous.
